t: ‘Bland, faintly sugary and cardboardy’: the best (and worst) supermarket porridge oats, tasted and rated
lede: Which get the day off to a satisfying start – and which make for a gruelling breakfast?

img.cap: ‘A high bar across the board.’ Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.

p: In the winter of 2003-04, my girlfriend and I hosted a Scottish family at a chalet in Val d’Isère. Full of chef bravado, I promised the father that I’d make him the best bowl of breakfast porridge he’d ever had. He, of course, turned up his nose at my bowl of sweet dessert, which I’d laced with cream and sugar, and showed me how to make porridge with just water and salt instead. I’ve never looked back.

In my experience, most jumbo oats need twice as much water as the packet instructions suggest, as well as three times as long to cook and turn satisfyingly creamy. Regular and vigorous stirring is essential, too, as is the sea salt, which turns a bland bowl of pap into a naturally sweet, earthy and nutty porridge.

For this test, I cooked each brand according to the recipe on the packet, using a 40g portion for most of them, but with varying quantities of water and cooking times (of course, adjust these to taste). The products are a mixture of porridge oats, which are cut before rolling, resulting in a creamier gruel that is quicker to cook, and jumbo rolled oats, which are rolled whole and take much longer to break down.

The organic oats were noticeably more flavourful than the conventionally grown ones, though that didn’t affect the texture, which seemed mostly dependent on the cut and the proportion of whole and broken flakes. With a high bar across the board, this test was a pleasure to judge, with most products scoring well.

body.h: Best overall: M&S organic traditional oats

p: A large paper bag of organic-certified Scottish oat flakes with a fresh, sweet, nutty aroma. Cooked for five minutes with 220ml water, the porridge is velvety with a tender bite, full-bodied and has a gentle, umami nuttiness.

A large paper bag of wholegrain British whole rolled oats from a family mill in Crewe with a strong green policy and its own wind turbine and solar farm. A wonderful, sweet aroma, too. When cooked for six minutes in 200ml water and rested for a minute, this is a dense porridge with a chewy, risotto-like texture and a mellow, rounded flavour.

body.h: And the rest … Tesco organic oats

p: A paper bag of organic-certified rolled oats with a vivid, sweet aroma, but no origin stated. Cook 50g oats with 300ml water for seven minutes to make a toothsome, chewy grain with a rich, full-bodied, earthy and complex flavour. Holds its shape, too, while many other brands collapse.

A large paper bag of Irish oat flakes from a family mill at Kilmacthomas, County Waterford. A fairly neutral aroma. Once cooked with 275ml water for four minutes, it makes a creamy, spoon-coating porridge in which sweetness dominates.

body.h: Co-op Irresistible Scottish jumbo rolled oats

p: A cardboard box containing a mixture of whole and broken flakes, with an earthy aroma. Cooked for seven minutes with 280ml water, the porridge is luscious with a soft, grainy bite and deliciously nutty flavour.

body.h: Glebe Farm PureOaty gluten-free organic porridge oats

p: A sealed plastic bag of gluten-free, organic-certified small rolled oats with a generous, sweet aroma. Cook with 250ml water for four minutes, leave to stand for two minutes more, and you get a smooth porridge with a fibrous texture, mellow sweetness and a deep, umami flavour. Locally grown, milled and packed at Glebe Farm in Cambridgeshire, with a strong green policy.

A cardboard box of jumbo rolled British oats with a familiar, sweet aroma. Cooked for five minutes with 195ml water, they develop a claggy, gluey consistency with plenty of texture and a deep, wholesome, earthy flavour. Quaker is owned by PepsiCo.

A plastic bag of small wholegrain oat flakes with a clean, nutty aroma. Cooked for four minutes with 270ml water, this is a creamy porridge with a little bite, a sweet scent of oat grain and a gentle, inoffensive flavour.

A paper bag of small rolled oat flakes with a rich, vanilla aroma. When cooked for four minutes with 285ml water, these end up as chewy, textured oats swimming in a watery sauce. The flavour isn’t any better, either: bland, faintly sugary and cardboardy flakes. No origin, but an unbeatable price.

A plump paper bag of wholegrain oat flakes. Cooked for five minutes with 300ml water, they turn into a thin but well-combined porridge with a silky texture, a delicate sweetness and a familiarly comforting, quietly earthy flavour.
